display_title: Rules-Engine V&V and Monte Carlo Force-Pairing Analysis for a Tabletop Wargame
one_liner: A seeded, headless simulator of a full tabletop wargame ruleset, verified by conformance tests and replay determinism, used to run controlled Monte Carlo experiments on which force compositions win.
problem: Balance claims about force compositions (e.g. melee vs shooting armies) are usually anecdotal; a simulator can only answer them if it demonstrably implements the rules and its experiments control for list selection, seat order and opponent quality.
approach: Rule-numbered conformance ledger and 42 seeded test suites; reachability audits (implemented rules no driver could call); record/replay determinism as a conformance oracle; roster build audit; round-robin list tournaments with seats swapped, Bradley-Terry strength with bootstrap CIs; head-to-head policy duels with A/A and inverted positive controls and Wilson intervals; power calculations before tuning.
decision_relevance: Mirrors combat-model V&V and force-on-force analysis: shows how a plausible headline (melee wins 73%) was a sample-selection artifact, how silent input substitutions (wrong terrain, wrong mission) biased every batch result, and how controls bound what an AI-driven simulation can and cannot conclude.

headline_results.claim: The earlier 'melee wins 73%' figure was an artifact of sampling one army list per faction; within-archetype pairings were as lopsided as cross-archetype ones.

Whether melee beats shooting is NOT established: melee wins 61.5% of 239 decided cross-archetype games, but a list-level cluster bootstrap (13 lists, 2,000 resamples) gives [39.1, 82.1], which contains 50%. More lists, not more games, would settle it
Replay desync reduced to 0 of 1,535 recorded actions across six recordings, including two human games, after finding the headless tools were loading the wrong terrain and mission.
Roster importer audit: 0 of 9,190 models missing across 179 tournament lists (previously 64% missing in a sample, unevenly by faction).
Bradley-Terry list ordering stable across board settings (same top and bottom lists); list identity dominates archetype.

Of three AI heuristics, only stratagem use moved outcomes: 54.6% [50.6, 58.6] over 600 seat-swapped games vs an A/A control of 50.7%; an inverted-objective control lost at 44.6% [40.6, 48.6], bounding headroom for objective valuation.
Five implemented-and-tested rules were unreachable by any driver (reserves, transports, objective actions, surge moves, infiltrate) and were wired in.
headline_results.evidence: README 'Rules that existed but nothing could reach'; GLIDEPATH §3E

headline_results.claim: Test suites pass headless and seeded : 39 of 42 run during audit, 0 failed in 125 s (3 long soak suites skipped).

limitations: AI opponent is a greedy one-ply scorer; outcomes partly measure its blind spots.
Units are single oriented footprints, not player-placed models; no true line of sight.
List ranking is not validated against real tournament outcomes (corpus is undefeated or X-1 lists).
Archetype effect estimate is sensitive to terrain and mission scoring (55% to 64%) and its CI treats games, not lists, as independent.
Terrain transcriptions describe a superseded August 2026 card revision that cannot be re-obtained.
Base sizes, deployment maps and 8 layouts are invented; all rules/points data is third-party and not redistributed.
tech: Python 3 (serve, data build, RL bridge with numpy)
blockers_before_featuring: OWNER DECISION: publisher-derived terrain transcriptions remain in git history (now untracked), and missions/*.mission are still tracked. Publish from a fresh history, publish as-is, or feature as a write-up only
The other three settings (55.5 / 58.4 / 64.4%) still carry game-level intervals only; each needs a ~20-minute re-run with the cluster bootstrap
No pinned corpus snapshot, so balance tables are reproducible by seed on one machine only
